description: Mixtura-owned ingredient data for the seed (docs/seed-data.md). roles: role rules by tree node, applied by scripts/seed/roles.ts, null marks a node left unclassified. classics: property values added only when the checked classics are computed (packages/engine/vectors/classics), not written into the seed. Every entry names a source or has basis assumption; acidRange, where present, keeps the spread of the sources read, acid is the value used.

lemon-juice.source: Penniston KL, Nakada SY, Holmes RP, Assimos DG: Quantitative assessment of citric acid in lemon juice, lime juice, and commercially-available fruit juice products. J Endourol 22(3):567-570 (2008), doi:10.1089/end.2007.0304, PMC2637791 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2637791/), Table 1; single measured values cited as facts, the table is not copied
lemon-juice.note: Citric acid by ion chromatography, not titratable acidity: other acids are not counted, so the figure is a lower bound of the titratable acidity; citric acid is the acid the paper describes as concentrated in citrus fruits. Lemon juice, fresh from fruit: 48.0 g/l (SD 3.82, n = 2) = 4.80 g per 100 ml. The same table gives 34.1 and 39.2 g/l for two lemon juice concentrates; those are not fresh juice and are not used. Replaces the assumed 6.

lime-juice.source: Penniston KL, Nakada SY, Holmes RP, Assimos DG: Quantitative assessment of citric acid in lemon juice, lime juice, and commercially-available fruit juice products. J Endourol 22(3):567-570 (2008), doi:10.1089/end.2007.0304, PMC2637791 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2637791/), Table 1; single measured values cited as facts, the table is not copied
lime-juice.note: Citric acid by ion chromatography, not titratable acidity: other acids are not counted, so the figure is a lower bound of the titratable acidity; citric acid is the acid the paper describes as concentrated in citrus fruits. Lime juice, fresh from fruit: 45.8 g/l (SD 6.86, n = 2) = 4.58 g per 100 ml; the paper finds no difference from lemon juice (P = 0.35). A lime juice concentrate is 35.4 g/l, not used. Replaces the assumed 6.

orange-juice.source: Penniston KL, Nakada SY, Holmes RP, Assimos DG: Quantitative assessment of citric acid in lemon juice, lime juice, and commercially-available fruit juice products. J Endourol 22(3):567-570 (2008), doi:10.1089/end.2007.0304, PMC2637791 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2637791/), Table 1; single measured values cited as facts, the table is not copied
orange-juice.note: Citric acid by ion chromatography, not titratable acidity: other acids are not counted, so the figure is a lower bound of the titratable acidity; citric acid is the acid the paper describes as concentrated in citrus fruits. Orange juice, fresh from fruit: 9.10 g/l (SD 1.98, n = 2) = 0.91 g per 100 ml, the value used (bar practice squeezes fresh juice). Two ready-to-consume juices are 16.9 and 16.7 g/l; the paper finds fresh juice lower (P = 0.003). Range 0.91 to 1.69 keeps both.

grapefruit-juice.source: Penniston KL, Nakada SY, Holmes RP, Assimos DG: Quantitative assessment of citric acid in lemon juice, lime juice, and commercially-available fruit juice products. J Endourol 22(3):567-570 (2008), doi:10.1089/end.2007.0304, PMC2637791 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2637791/), Table 1; single measured values cited as facts, the table is not copied
grapefruit-juice.note: Citric acid by ion chromatography, not titratable acidity: other acids are not counted, so the figure is a lower bound of the titratable acidity; citric acid is the acid the paper describes as concentrated in citrus fruits. Grapefruit juice, ready-to-consume (one product, n = 1): 25.0 g/l = 2.50 g per 100 ml. The source has no fresh grapefruit juice; the value is that of a packaged juice.

pineapple-juice.source: Yusufali Z, Follett P, Wall M, et al.: Physiochemical and Sensory Properties of a Turmeric, Ginger, and Pineapple Functional Beverage with Effects of Pulp Content. Foods 13(5):718 (2024), doi:10.3390/foods13050718, PMC10931241, Table 2 (CC BY 4.0); and Sun X, Follett PA, Wall MM, et al.: Physical, Chemical, and Sensory Properties of a Turmeric-Fortified Pineapple Juice Beverage. Foods 12(12):2323 (2023), doi:10.3390/foods12122323, PMC10297280, Table 1 (CC BY 4.0)
pineapple-juice.note: Titratable acidity in % as the papers report it, measured with a digital acidity meter (ATAGO GMK-835F); the papers do not say in the read text which acid it is expressed as. Yusufali 2024: juice of a fresh pineapple, 0.57 ± 0.01 % (high and low pulp), the value used. Sun 2023: pasteurised pineapple puree juice, 0.52 ± 0.02 %. Range 0.52 to 0.57 keeps both.
